Yes — for a small private friend group, you can host and use this for free with persistent data.

Recommended setup:

- **Vercel Hobby** for the web app and API
- **Supabase Free** for persistent Postgres data, login, and optional receipt storage
- **GitHub** for source control and automatic Vercel deployments

This is easily enough for a typical friend group: Supabase Free includes a 500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users, and 1 GB storage. The main caveat is that an inactive free Supabase project pauses after one week; the data remains, but the first use after that may require it to resume. [Supabase pricing](https://supabase.com/pricing)

Vercel Hobby is $0 and supports a personal, non-commercial project, with HTTPS, deployments, and generous monthly request/function limits. It fits a private expense-sharing app well. If you turned it into a paid/public product, you’d need Vercel Pro. [Vercel Hobby terms and limits](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby)

We do **not** need anything from Splitwise’s GitHub repositories to build this. The repos you listed are mostly internal libraries or API documentation, not their full Splitwise product. I’d build an independent app with our own UI, database schema, calculations, and branding—so no dependency on Splitwise code, trademarks, or API.

Useful input from you before coding:

- Your must-have features: groups, equal/custom/percentage splits, settlements, recurring expenses, receipt uploads, reminders, etc.
- Login preference: email OTP, Google sign-in, or simple invite links.
- Preferred app name and visual style.
- Whether you need migration from your existing Splitwise balances. If yes, export your Splitwise data and share the CSV/JSON format—not GitHub repos.

Built the first working version of **Tally** in the workspace.

It includes:

- Google OAuth sign-in
- Bootstrap admins via `ADMIN_EMAILS`
- Admin console to approve, remove, promote, and demote users
- Private groups, approved-member additions, equal-split expenses
- Personal net balances and recorded settlements
- Supabase database schema with row-level access controls
- Vercel/Supabase deployment instructions

Start with [README.md](./README.md) and run the SQL migration at [001_initial.sql](./supabase/migrations/001_initial.sql).

I couldn’t run the build locally because Node/npm isn’t installed in this environment. Once Node is available, run:

```powershell
npm install
npm run build
```

The best ways to make it better than Splitwise, in my view:

- **UPI-first settlement:** show Paytm/GPay/PhonePe deep links and mark payment complete after confirmation.
- **Smarter settlement plans:** minimize transfers across a whole group, with a clear “why this payment” explanation.
- **Receipt-first entry:** upload a bill, extract items, then let people claim their own items.
- **Trips mode:** budgets, multi-currency expenses, daily spending summary, and a final settle-up view.
- **No nagging, better reminders:** gentle, configurable reminders only when a balance is meaningful or old.
- **Transparent privacy:** no ads, no social graph, simple export/delete controls, and full group audit history.

The next worthwhile feature to implement is custom/itemized/percentage splits; equal split is intentionally the initial baseline.

The production build completed successfully — the app is ready to deploy.

The TypeScript config changes are normal Next.js additions.

Don’t run `npm audit fix --force` blindly; it can introduce breaking dependency upgrades. The next step is configuring Supabase, Google OAuth, and Vercel using [README.md](./README.md).

> i wanna check the ui and all locally first

Run this in the project folder:

```powershell
npm run dev
```

Then open http://localhost:3000.

The landing page will render immediately. To test sign-in, groups, expenses, and admin controls, first create `.env.local` from `.env.example` and fill in your Supabase values, then run the SQL migration and configure Google OAuth as described in [README.md](./README.md).

For your own local account to become the first admin, set:

```env
ADMIN_EMAILS=your-google-email@gmail.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=http://localhost:3000
```

After saving `.env.local`, stop the dev server with `Ctrl+C` and run `npm run dev` again.

I’ll deploy the app directly to Vercel. The initial deployment can go live now, but the Google sign-in and database features will become functional after we add the Supabase environment variables and OAuth redirect URL in the Vercel/Supabase dashboards.

> i will deploy. ytell me how to

1. Go to [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new) and sign in with GitHub.

2. Since this folder isn’t a Git repo yet, create a GitHub repository, then run in `D:\Timepass\anti-kothari`:

```powershell
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Tally app"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/tally.git
git push -u origin main
```

3. Back in Vercel, select the `tally` repository and click **Deploy**. Vercel detects Next.js automatically; leave the defaults.

4. After deploying, go to Vercel project → **Settings → Environment Variables** and add:

```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=...
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=...
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=...
ADMIN_EMAILS=your-google-email@gmail.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://your-app.vercel.app
```

5. Create a Supabase project, open its SQL Editor, and run [001_initial.sql](./supabase/migrations/001_initial.sql).

6. In Supabase → **Authentication → Providers → Google**, enable Google OAuth and add the Google credentials from Google Cloud Console.

7. In Supabase → **Authentication → URL Configuration**, set:

- Site URL: `https://your-app.vercel.app`
- Redirect URL: `https://your-app.vercel.app/auth/callback`

8. Redeploy from Vercel after adding the variables.

For a first quick UI preview, deploy before steps 4–7; the landing page loads, but sign-in won’t work until Supabase is configured.

> how to deploy in vercel

1. Open [Vercel](https://vercel.com) and sign in with your GitHub account.

2. Click **Add New… → Project**.

3. If your code is not on GitHub yet:
   - Create a new repository at [github.com/new](https://github.com/new).
   - In `D:\Timepass\anti-kothari`, run:

```powershell
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Tally app"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/tally.git
git push -u origin main
```

4. Back on Vercel, click **Import** beside the `tally` repository.

5. Confirm:
   - Framework Preset: **Next.js**
   - Root Directory: `./`
   - Build Command: `npm run build`

6. Click **Deploy**.

Vercel will build it and give you a live URL like `https://tally-xxx.vercel.app`.

At this stage, the homepage works. Add Supabase environment variables and Google OAuth afterward to make login and data storage work.

> now lets set up supabase and everything

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

> I’ll walk you through the full production setup in the right order: Supabase database, Google OAuth, Vercel variables, then a live sign-in test. I’m checking the current official setup details so the callback URLs and keys are exact.
>

Set it up in this order. Your app name is already configurable with `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME=anti-kothari`.

1. Create a Supabase project

- Go to [Supabase](https://supabase.com/dashboard), sign in, and click **New project**.
- Pick an organization, name it `anti-kothari`, choose a database password, and create it.
- Wait until the project is ready.

2. Create the database schema

- In Supabase, open **SQL Editor → New query**.
- Open [001_initial.sql](./supabase/migrations/001_initial.sql) locally.
- Copy all its contents into Supabase’s SQL Editor and click **Run**.

This creates the expense tables, profiles, role/approval system, and security policies.

3. Get your Supabase credentials

In Supabase, open **Settings → API Keys**:

- Copy **Project URL** → `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`
- Copy the **Publishable key** (`sb_publishable_...`) → `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`
- Copy the **Secret key** (`sb_secret_...`) → `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`

The publishable/secret keys are Supabase’s current preferred key types; do not expose the secret key anywhere public. [Supabase API-key guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/api-keys)

4. Add Vercel environment variables

Go to Vercel → your `anti-kothari` project → **Settings → Environment Variables**.

Add these for **Production**, **Preview**, and **Development**:

```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=your-project-url
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=your-publishable-key
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=your-secret-key
ADMIN_EMAILS=your-google-email@gmail.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://anti-kothari.vercel.app
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME=anti-kothari
```

Use your own Google email in `ADMIN_EMAILS`. You can add multiple initial admins separated by commas.

5. Configure Supabase redirect URLs

In Supabase → **Authentication → URL Configuration**:

- Site URL:

```text
https://anti-kothari.vercel.app
```

- Add these Redirect URLs:

```text
https://anti-kothari.vercel.app/auth/callback
http://localhost:3000/auth/callback
```

Supabase requires the `redirectTo` URL used by the app to be on this allow-list. [Supabase redirect URL documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/redirect-urls)

6. Configure Google OAuth

In Supabase → **Authentication → Providers → Google**, copy the displayed callback URL. It will look like:

```text
https://YOUR-PROJECT-REF.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback
```

Then open [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/):

- Create/select a project.
- Open **Google Auth Platform**.
- Configure the consent screen/branding.
- Create an OAuth Client ID of type **Web application**.
- Add Authorized JavaScript Origins:

```text
https://anti-kothari.vercel.app
http://localhost:3000
```

- Add the Supabase callback URL you copied above under **Authorized redirect URIs**.
- Copy the Google Client ID and Client Secret into Supabase’s Google provider settings, enable the provider, and save.

These are the current required Google/Supabase OAuth settings. [Supabase’s Google OAuth guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/social-login/auth-google)

7. Redeploy and test

In Vercel → **Deployments**, open the newest deployment’s `…` menu and choose **Redeploy**. Environment-variable changes apply only to new deployments. [Vercel environment variables](https://vercel.com/docs/environment-variables)

Then:

- Open `https://anti-kothari.vercel.app/login`
- Sign in with the Google email listed in `ADMIN_EMAILS`
- You should enter as an approved admin
- Other people can sign in, but appear in **Admin → Awaiting approval** until you approve them.

- Secret key → `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`

Keep the secret key private; paste it only into Vercel’s Environment Variables page.

> should i publish the app?

For your private friend group, **don’t publish it yet**.

Keep the Google OAuth app in **Testing** mode and add all friend emails under **Test users**. This is safer and avoids unnecessary Google verification.

Publish it only if you want people outside your listed test users to sign in. Publishing changes the app to production access and may require Google verification depending on the scopes and configuration.

Your Vercel deployment is already publicly reachable; “publishing” here refers specifically to the Google OAuth consent screen.

You don’t need to add every friend manually.

Our app only uses Google’s basic identity scopes:

```text
openid
email
profile
```

Google explicitly exempts apps requesting only these sign-in scopes from the test-user allowlist, even while the app is in Testing mode. Friends should be able to sign in without being individually added. [Google Cloud audience rules](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549945)

So leave the app in **Testing** for now. This avoids publishing/verification while still allowing normal Google sign-in.

If Google still blocks a particular account, add that account as a test user temporarily. Don’t publish unless you later add Google API access beyond basic login or want a fully public production OAuth app.

> it still deos not have the full spectrum of features of splitwise

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> You’re right—the current build is a polished core, not Splitwise parity. I’ll map the missing product surface and separate “must-have parity” from optional enhancements so we can close the gaps in the right order.
</details>

You’re right. What we have today is a polished MVP, not a full Splitwise replacement.

Current limitations:

- Equal splits only
- One payer per expense
- INR only
- No custom, percentage, shares, or itemized splitting
- No expense editing or deletion
- No recurring expenses
- No receipts or attachments
- No comments or activity history
- No email/invite links
- No reminders or notifications
- No proper debt simplification algorithm
- No partial settlements or payment links
- No multi-currency support
- No data export/import
- No audit log

The correct next build sequence is:

1. Custom split engine: equal, exact amounts, percentages, shares, itemized expenses, multiple payers.
2. Proper balances: net balances per person and minimized settlement transfers.
3. Expense lifecycle: edit, delete, categories, notes, dates, recurring expenses.
4. Group management: invite links, pending invitations, member removal, roles.
5. Receipts and history: image uploads, comments, audit trail, CSV export.
6. Notifications: balance reminders, new expenses, approvals, settlements.
7. Multi-currency and trip mode.
8. UPI/payment links and settlement confirmation.

I’d start with steps 1–3 because they are the core parity features and require a database migration, not just UI work. The current schema is intentionally too simple for them.

A few things worth a second look:

- Should the app support currencies beyond INR from the first major upgrade?
- Should receipt uploads use Supabase Storage, or should we keep the first version text-only?
- Do you want automatic email reminders, or should reminders remain inside the app?

> why is the app soooo damn slow to load in everything

Because every click currently waits on a server round-trip before showing the next screen.

The main causes in this app are:

- **Vercel/Supabase region distance:** your logs showed Vercel routing execution through Washington, DC while you’re in India. If the Supabase database is also in a US region, each request travels India → US → India.
- **Server-rendered pages:** dashboard, groups, admin, and group pages fetch authentication and database data on every navigation.
- **Too many database calls:** one dashboard load fetches memberships, then expense and settlement data for every group. I made those parallel, but it still needs consolidating into one database query/RPC.
- **No client cache yet:** revisiting a group repeats requests instead of instantly showing cached data.
- **Vercel Hobby cold starts:** inactive server functions can take extra time on the first request.

The proper fix is:

1. Put Supabase in Mumbai/Singapore and Vercel functions in Mumbai.
2. Replace dashboard/group balance calculations with one Supabase RPC.
3. Add client-side caching/prefetching for groups and expenses.
4. Keep the loading skeleton, but show cached content immediately.
5. Avoid fetching `currentProfile()` separately in every nested server component.

Right now the app is functioning like a server-rendered website, not a responsive app. The next engineering pass should be performance architecture, not more UI changes.

Do this carefully:

  - one-year auth cookie settings
